entities.name: Muḥammad b. Ibrāhīm b. Saʿīd S̲h̲ams al-dīn Abū ʿAbda al-Anṣārī
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Muḥammad b. Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿīd Shams al-dīn Abū ʿAbda al-Anṣārī, a Kurdish Cairene encyclopedist and physician from the Medieval era, played a pivotal role in shaping Islamic knowledge and culture during the 14th century. His contributions to medicine, philosophy, and literature helped spread knowledge across the Middle East and North Africa.

 Born in unknown circumstances, Abū ʿAbda al-Anṣārī dedicated his life to compiling and disseminating encyclopedic works, including the influential manuscript 'Kitab al-mansum'. His work on medical texts, such as the treatise 'Tawdih al-qanun', earned him recognition among Islamic scholars. The historian Ibn Khaldun often cited Abū ʿAbda's philosophical writings in his own works.

 Despite the challenges of his time, including the Black Death and conflicts between regional powers, Abū ʿAbda's legacy endured through his meticulous documentation and transmission of knowledge. His impact on Islamic scholarship can be seen in the works of subsequent scholars and continues to inspire research today.

 The sheer breadth of his writings, encompassing subjects from medicine to literature, testifies to his boundless curiosity and intellectual pursuits.

entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Muḥammad b. Ibrāhīm b. Saʿīd S̲h̲ams al-dīn Abū ʿAbda al-Anṣārī, better known as Ibn al-Akfānī, was a prolific Kurdish-Cairene polymath, physician, and encyclopedist whose intellectual contributions spanned the Mamluk Sultanate during the first half of the 14th century (c. 1286–1348 CE). Born in Sinjar, Upper Mesopotamia, he became a central figure in the vibrant scholarly milieu of Cairo, serving as a physician at the prestigious al-Mansuri Hospital and leaving behind a corpus of works that systematically categorized and transmitted knowledge across diverse fields. His magnum opus, *Irshād al-qāṣid ilā asnā al-maqāṣid* ('Guide for the Seeker to the Noblest Aims'), stands as one of the most comprehensive and influential encyclopedias of its era, reflecting the intellectual zenith of Mamluk Egypt.

Ibn al-Akfānī's literary output was characterized by its encyclopedic ambition and meticulous organization. Beyond the *Irshād*, which systemized over 100 branches of knowledge from theology and philosophy to medicine and mineralogy, he authored specialized treatises such as *Nihāyat al-suʼl wa-al-umniyah fī taʻallum aʻmāl al-furūsīyah* ('The Utmost Quest and Desire for Learning the Arts of Horsemanship'), a detailed manual on Mamluk military arts, including equestrianism, archery, and sword fighting. His medical works, like *Kashf al-rayn fī amrāḍ al-ʿayn* (on ophthalmology) and *Durrat al-ghawwāṣ fī awhām al-khawāṣṣ* (on materia medica), demonstrated deep practical and theoretical knowledge, solidifying his reputation as a leading physician of his time.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ibn al-Akfānī's comprehensive encyclopedic works, particularly *Irshād al-qāṣid*, served as vital reservoirs of knowledge for centuries, directly influencing Mamluk and Ottoman scholarship. His detailed treatises on military arts also provide unparalleled insight into the Mamluk military system, a dominant force in the medieval Near East.
